label: Figure 1
title: Figure 1 · Study design and analytical workflow
legend: Overview of the KNHANES 2007–2024 study. a, Dataset preparation across 18 annual surveys: 140,372 participant records, 111,381 adults aged at least 19 years, 335 exposures and 149 quantitative phenotypes. Pair-specific eligibility required at least two compatible survey years and 500 complete observations, yielding 24,008 exposure–phenotype pairs, 26,078 coefficient contrasts and 100,556 contributing adults. b, Survey-weighted association screening, association profiles, 113 joint exposure models, exposure networks and atlas-wide vibration of effects across 12 optional adjustment factors and up to 64 model specifications per pair. Robustness analyses assessed annual recurrence, covariate sensitivity, age interactions and measurement consistency. c, Exposure information and complementarity, insulin-resistance indices and their components, physiological aging and subjective memory, and comparison with UK Biobank polygenic scores. d, Targeted biomarker, dietary and environmental extensions and external evaluation in NHANES, CHARLS and ELSA. External replication required the same association direction and Holm-adjusted P < 0.05. NHANES, US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey; CHARLS, China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study; ELSA, English Longitudinal Study of Ageing.

label: Figure 2
title: Figure 2 · Exposure–phenotype associations across the core atlas
legend: Top (a), bidirectional association plots for nine phenotype domains. Each point represents one of 26,078 coefficient contrasts from 24,008 exposure–phenotype pairs. Positive and negative coefficients appear above and below zero, respectively; distance from zero represents −log₁₀(P), capped at 20. Colors and the strips below each panel identify exposure categories. Filled colored points denote Bonferroni-adjusted P < 0.05 (1,716 contrasts), open colored points denote BY-adjusted P < 0.05 without Bonferroni significance (2,054), and gray points denote the remaining contrasts (22,308). Dashed lines mark the Bonferroni threshold. Both corrections use the full 26,078-contrast family. Bottom, horizontal bars show the percentage of Bonferroni-significant coefficients by phenotype domain (b) and exposure category (c); N gives the number of tested coefficients in each group. Estimates came from survey-weighted linear models with demographic, socioeconomic, survey-year and applicable exposure-specific adjustment. Continuous exposures were log₁₀-transformed and standardized, ordinal exposures were modeled per score increment, and categorical exposures were compared with their reference groups. Phenotypes were expressed in standard deviation units.

label: Figure 3
title: Figure 3 · Atlas of standardized exposure–phenotype coefficients
legend: Left (a), heat map of 26,078 estimated coefficients arranged in 361 exposure-contrast rows and 149 phenotype columns. Rows and columns follow the predefined exposure categories and phenotype domains. Categorical levels and distinct reference definitions retain separate rows. Right, enlarged strips show four nutrient-biomarker rows (b) and five environmental-chemical rows (c) across the same phenotype columns; arrows identify selected phenotypes. Blue and red indicate negative and positive coefficients, respectively, and white indicates values near zero. Color intensity follows asinh(β/0.03), with a common legend labeled on the original coefficient scale and color limits of −0.6 and 0.6. Gray cells indicate combinations without an estimated coefficient. All estimated coefficients are shown irrespective of statistical significance, and the ordering follows the catalog. Coefficients represent phenotype standard deviation units per standard deviation of log₁₀-transformed continuous exposure, per ordinal score increment, or relative to the categorical reference. BMD, bone mineral density; FEV1, forced expiratory volume in 1 s; LC-MS/MS, liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry; RIA, radioimmunoassay.

label: Figure 4
title: Figure 4 · Single-exposure and joint exposure contributions to phenotypic variance
legend: Top (a), distributions of single-exposure incremental weighted R² across nine phenotype domains, grouped by exposure category; the vertical ΔR² axis uses a square-root scale. Red indicates Bonferroni-significant overall tests, green indicates BY significance without Bonferroni significance, and blue indicates the remaining pairs. The 24,008 pairs comprise 1,704 Bonferroni-significant, 1,944 additional BY-significant and 20,360 remaining pairs. Bottom left (b) and middle (c), empirical cumulative distributions of ΔR² by significance group, with median ΔR² annotations for Bonferroni-significant pairs by phenotype domain and exposure category, respectively; these panels display ΔR² from 0 to 0.05. Bottom right (d), weighted R² of covariate-only models versus exposure-expanded models for 24,008 single-exposure pairs (gray) and 113 joint exposure models (red; Supplementary Table 11). The dashed line denotes equal R². Joint models contain up to 20 BY-selected exposures; results were averaged across ten completed datasets when imputation was required. Each ΔR² comparison uses identical participants and survey weights. Supplementary Table 12 provides the five clinical models and their complete-case comparisons.

label: Figure 5
title: Figure 5 · Exposure correlation networks and their distributions
legend: Chord diagrams show the random exposure network (upper left, a), the GGT exposure network (lower left, c) and the systolic blood pressure network (lower right, d). The random panel contains 50 exposures expanded to 58 nodes and 46 correlations with |r| > 0.25. The GGT panel displays 19 scalar exposures and 18 such correlations in 2,439 past-year drinkers from 2010–2011; the categorical smoking term is retained in the joint model but is not a scalar node in this panel. The blood pressure panel contains seven exposures and four correlations in 8,980 adults aged 19–64 years from 2014–2016. Outer-sector colors identify exposure categories, ribbon colors distinguish correlation direction, and ribbon width represents |r|. Selected nodes without a qualifying correlation are retained. GGT and blood pressure correlations are panel-specific weighted partial correlations averaged on the Fisher-z scale across ten completed datasets. Upper right (b), empirical cumulative distributions contain 995 random-panel correlations, 171 GGT correlations, 21 blood pressure correlations and 17,555 core-atlas Bonferroni-significant correlations from 64,556 planned comparisons. Vertical dashed lines mark r = −0.25 and 0.25. The node key defines all displayed abbreviations. GGT, gamma-glutamyl transferase; SBP, systolic blood pressure.

label: Extended Data Figure 1
title: Extended Data Figure 1 · Survey-weighted atlas construction and environmental extension
legend: Analytical workflow for the core KNHANES atlas and the July 2020–August 2021 environmental survey. The core analysis paired 335 exposures with 149 quantitative phenotypes across 18 annual surveys, requiring compatible measurements, component-specific weights, at least two survey years and at least 500 complete observations. Continuous exposures were log₁₀-transformed and scaled by weighted standard deviations; quantitative phenotypes were standardized from their original scale. Survey-weighted linear models incorporated strata, primary sampling units and applicable covariates. Summary statistics included β, SE, P values, R², ΔR² and Bonferroni and BY corrections. Robustness analyses assessed annual recurrence, I², age interactions and covariate sensitivity. Vibration-of-effects analyses evaluated all eligible atlas pairs across 12 optional adjustment factors and up to 64 specifications per pair. Joint models included up to 20 BY-selected exposures and ten completed datasets where imputation was required. The separate environmental branch evaluated 19 indicators against 23 phenotypes using survey-specific weights and a 437-hypothesis family. PSU, primary sampling unit.

label: Extended Data Figure 2
title: Extended Data Figure 2 · Correlations between exposure and phenotype association profiles
legend: Upper heat map (a), Pearson correlations between the phenotype association profiles of 361 exposure contrasts. Lower heat map (b), Pearson correlations between the exposure association profiles of 149 phenotypes. Profiles were constructed from the core coefficient matrix: estimated coefficients with nominal P ≥ 0.10 were set to zero, while unestimated cells remained missing. Each correlation required at least 20 shared measured coefficients. Orange and blue-green indicate positive and negative profile correlations, respectively, and white indicates values near zero. Gray denotes unavailable correlations because of insufficient overlap or zero profile variance. Rows and columns retain the predefined domain ordering.

label: Extended Data Figure 3
title: Extended Data Figure 3 · Annual recurrence of pooled associations
legend: Distributions of the number of survey years with nominal P < 0.05 among 3,770 coefficient contrasts significant under BY adjustment in the pooled core atlas. Panels group contrasts by the number of years with an eligible annual estimate, ranging from two to 18 years. Panel n values count coefficient contrasts. Horizontal bar lengths and labels give the percentage within each panel; the darkest bars mark the highest percentage, and open circles indicate zero. Annual models used compatible exposure and phenotype definitions, survey-specific weights and within-year standardization; 25,971 annual estimates contributed. Recurrence counts are based on annual significance without a same-direction requirement.

label: Extended Data Figure 4
title: Extended Data Figure 4 · Age-dependent associations and additional explained variance
legend: Upper left (a), distribution of the exposure coefficient at age 40 minus that at age 70. Upper right (b), distribution of the original coefficient from the model without interaction minus the coefficient at age 70 from the interaction model. Both panels include 1,519 of the 1,716 Bonferroni-significant coefficient contrasts whose observed age ranges supported both ages. Lower panel (c), additional weighted R² after adding exposure × (age − 55) terms across all 24,008 eligible core pairs. Interaction models retained the primary covariates, including age and age squared, as well as the original participants, survey weights, transformations and scales. Age-specific coefficients were derived from the fitted main and interaction terms.

label: Extended Data Figure 5
title: Extended Data Figure 5 · Atlas-wide vibration of association effects
legend: Vibration-of-effects analysis of 26,078 coefficient contrasts from all 24,008 eligible exposure–phenotype pairs, using 12 optional adjustment factors and up to 64 specifications per pair. a, Empirical cumulative distributions of the range of β across specifications for 1,716 atlas Bonferroni-significant coefficients and 24,362 other coefficients; the horizontal axis is logarithmic. b, Percentages retaining nominal significance in every model, retaining Bonferroni significance in at least half of models, changing sign, or attaining nominal significance in opposite directions. c–e, Examples for 25-hydroxyvitamin D₃ and BMI, blood lead and HDL cholesterol, and beer frequency and GGT. Left, changes in |β| associated with including each adjustment factor, estimated across specifications. Right, β versus −log₁₀(P) for 64 specifications, shown separately for the two largest absolute adjustment contributions. Orange indicates inclusion of the named factor and blue indicates its absence; diamonds mark the primary model refitted in the common sample. Solid and dashed horizontal lines mark P = 0.05 and P = 0.05/26,078, respectively. Within each pair, participants, survey design and variable scales were held fixed. Full summaries are provided in Supplementary Table 9. BMI, body mass index; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; GGT, gamma-glutamyl transferase.

label: Extended Data Figure 6
title: Extended Data Figure 6 · Sensitivity of association coefficients to covariate adjustment
legend: Upper panels (a), distributions of the primary-model coefficient minus the coefficient under each comparison specification for 1,716 Bonferroni-significant core contrasts. Base models retained survey year and applicable energy or urinary-creatinine adjustment. The other specifications added age and age squared, sex, both age terms and sex, or household income and education, as labeled. Primary models included all applicable adjustment terms. Lower panel (b), HDL cholesterol associations with blood lead (purple), total fat intake from 24-h recall (gold) and walking days per week (teal) across six specifications. Points and horizontal intervals indicate standardized coefficients and individual-model 95% confidence intervals. Each within-pair comparison retained the same participants, survey design, transformations, standardization and categorical references. HDL, high-density lipoprotein.

label: Extended Data Figure 7
title: Extended Data Figure 7 · Exposome and polygenic-score increments in explained variance
legend: Comparison of KNHANES joint-exposure ΔR² (vertical axis) with published polygenic risk score (PRS) ΔR² in the white British UK Biobank test set (horizontal axis; Tanigawa et al., 2022, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pgen.1010105). Six points represent five clinical phenotypes; the two direct low-density lipoprotein cholesterol panels use different KNHANES measurement periods and share the same genetic benchmark. Labels give the KNHANES years and number of jointly modeled exposures. Colors denote liver, lipid and kidney phenotypes. The dashed line denotes equal ΔR². KNHANES values are in-sample, survey-weighted increments over covariate-only models, averaged across ten completed datasets. UK Biobank values summarize incremental performance in a held-out sample. The urine-albumin model used limit-of-detection substitution. LDL, low-density lipoprotein; LOD, limit of detection.

label: Extended Data Figure 8
title: Extended Data Figure 8 · Association correspondence across dietary and biomarker measurements
legend: a, Coefficients for 814 matched nutrient–phenotype associations measured by 24-h recall (horizontal axis) and food-frequency questionnaire (FFQ; vertical axis), covering 22 nutrients and 37 phenotypes. b–d, Circulating-biomarker associations (horizontal axes) versus corresponding dietary-nutrient associations (vertical axes): serum vitamin A and dietary retinol (35 comparisons), serum vitamin E and dietary vitamin E (35), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D₃ and dietary vitamin D (33). Orange, teal and purple identify Bonferroni-significant, BY-significant-only and nonsignificant horizontal-axis associations, respectively, using the original 26,078-contrast family. Diagonal dashed lines indicate equal coefficients; horizontal and vertical lines indicate zero. Marginal curves show within-group density distributions of the coefficients; groups with fewer than ten comparisons are represented by ticks. Each coefficient retains its measurement-specific eligible sample and standardization. 25(OH)D3, 25-hydroxyvitamin D₃.

label: Extended Data Figure 9
title: Extended Data Figure 9 · Correlation network of exposures associated with lung function
legend: Chord diagram of 14 exposures associated with forced expiratory volume in 1 s in the 2007–2019 measurement series, selected from Bonferroni-significant pairs by single-exposure ΔR². Expansion of smoking status yields 16 nodes. Twelve ribbons meet both r > 0.25 and Bonferroni significance across the 64,556 planned exposure-node comparisons. Ribbon width represents r; colors identify exposure categories. Five nodes without a qualifying correlation are retained. Correlations use survey-weighted demographic- and socioeconomic-adjusted exposure-pair samples. Node abbreviations: Energy, total energy intake; Food amt., total food intake; Food water, water from foods; Vit C FFQ, vitamin C intake from the food-frequency questionnaire; Beer freq., beer consumption frequency; KHEI orig., Korean Healthy Eating Index using the 2013–2018 definition; Vig. days, vigorous activity days per week; Vig. GPAQ, vigorous leisure activity from the Global Physical Activity Questionnaire; Str. exer., muscle-strengthening frequency; Flex. exer., flexibility exercise frequency; Educ., education; Inc. HH, household-income quartile; Inc. SA, sex- and age-specific income quartile. Smoking nodes denote never-established (<100 lifetime cigarettes), former and current established smoking.

label: Supplementary Figure 1
title: Supplementary Figure 1 · Demographic composition of annual analysis samples
legend: Survey-weighted demographic summaries of pair-specific analysis samples by KNHANES survey year, 2007–2024. Panels show mean age (a), the percentage of female participants (b), four education categories (c) and four household-income quartiles (d). Within each year, red points mark the 10th and 90th percentiles, black points the 25th and 75th percentiles, and blue open diamonds the median across pair-specific summaries. Pairs receive equal weight when calculating these percentiles; survey weights are used within each pair-specific summary. The figure includes 111,110 annual pair-specific samples belonging to the final 24,008 exposure–phenotype pairs, with adult eligibility, complete model covariates and the corresponding measurement and weight requirements. Q1–Q4, lowest through highest household-income quartiles.

label: Supplementary Figure 2
title: Supplementary Figure 2 · Distributions of association P values
legend: Distributions of unadjusted two-sided P values for the 26,078 coefficient contrasts in the core exposure–phenotype atlas. Upper panels (a) group contrasts into seven exposure categories, and lower panels (b) into nine phenotype domains. Gray histograms use 30 equal-width bins over P = 0–1 and are scaled to density within each group; black lines show Gaussian kernel density estimates. Each coefficient contributes once within its category, including separate contrasts for categorical exposures. All estimated contrasts are included, irrespective of multiple-testing significance. P-E, phenotype–exposure.

label: Supplementary Figure 3
title: Supplementary Figure 3 · Exposure associations and shared profiles for glycated hemoglobin
legend: Upper left (a), incremental weighted R² against −log₁₀(P) for 268 exposure–glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) pairs; ΔR² is expressed in percentage points. Upper right (b), 285 exposure coefficients against −log₁₀(P), expressed in HbA1c standard deviation units. Circles denote one standard deviation of continuous exposure, triangles one ordinal score increment, and squares a category versus its reference. Orange indicates Bonferroni significance, teal Benjamini–Yekutieli significance only, and gray-blue the remaining estimates. Dashed horizontal lines mark the Bonferroni thresholds for the full 24,008-pair family on the left and 26,078-contrast family on the right. Lower panel (c), the 40 strongest absolute correlations between the HbA1c exposure profile and profiles of other phenotypes. Profile construction follows Extended Data Figure 2; orange and teal bars indicate positive and negative correlations. DXA, dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; IRMA, immunoradiometric assay; SD, standard deviation.

label: Supplementary Figure 4
title: Supplementary Figure 4 · Between-year heterogeneity of association coefficients
legend: Distributions of I² among 3,770 core coefficient contrasts significant under Benjamini–Yekutieli adjustment, grouped by exposure category. Heterogeneity was calculated from 25,971 eligible annual estimates covering two to 18 years per contrast using inverse-variance weighting and Cochran’s Q. I² is displayed as a proportion from zero to one. Boxes span the 25th–75th percentiles, central lines indicate medians, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 interquartile ranges; gray points show individual contrasts. Categorical exposure contrasts were evaluated separately using their aligned annual estimates.

label: Supplementary Figure 5
title: Supplementary Figure 5 · Changes in coefficients after full covariate adjustment
legend: Histograms of fully adjusted minus minimally adjusted coefficients for all 26,078 core contrasts from 24,008 exposure–phenotype pairs. Panels show the seven exposure categories, and n denotes the number of coefficient contrasts. Minimal models retained survey year and applicable energy-intake or urinary-creatinine terms; full models additionally included age, age squared, sex, education and household income, with exposure-equivalent covariates omitted. Each comparison used the same participants, survey weights, transformations, scales and categorical references. The histograms use 120 bins and common horizontal and vertical ranges across panels.

label: Supplementary Figure 6
title: Supplementary Figure 6 · Environmental exposure–phenotype associations and sensitivity analyses
legend: a, Standardized coefficients for 19 environmental indicators and 23 phenotypes in the July 2020–August 2021 KNHANES special survey. Red and blue indicate positive and negative associations. Asterisks indicate Benjamini–Yekutieli-adjusted P < 0.05 across 437 planned hypotheses. The gray cell denotes indoor benzene–neck circumference (n = 493), below the 500-participant threshold; 436 estimated models included 611–1,861 participants. Individual-level models used volatile organic compound survey weights, strata and primary sampling units, with demographic, socioeconomic and applicable urinary-creatinine adjustment. All exposures were log₁₀-transformed and standardized. AST, aspartate aminotransferase; BMI, body mass index; CO₂, carbon dioxide; HbA1c, glycated hemoglobin; HDL, high-density lipoprotein; PM2.5, particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter ≤2.5 μm; VOC, volatile organic compound. Urinary metabolite abbreviations are defined in the environmental metabolite key below.

b, Standardized coefficients and individual-model 95% confidence intervals for six urinary volatile organic compound–blood phenotype pairs significant under primary Benjamini–Yekutieli adjustment. Black denotes primary models; pink, additional smoking adjustment; blue, log₁₀ urinary-creatinine adjustment; and green, creatinine-normalized exposure concentrations. Every estimate uses 1,735 participants. Primary models included age, age squared, sex, education, income and original-scale urinary creatinine. The dashed vertical line marks zero. Multiplicity-adjusted P values are reported in Supplementary Table 8. BPMA, N-acetyl-S-(n-propyl)-L-cysteine; PGA, phenylglyoxylic acid; 3HPMA, N-acetyl-S-(3-hydroxypropyl)-L-cysteine; 2MHA, 2-methylhippuric acid; 34MHA, combined 3- and 4-methylhippuric acids.

c, Post hoc comparison of 27 urinary volatile organic compound–urinary phenotype pairs under original-scale (blue) and log₁₀ (pink) urinary-creatinine adjustment. Phenotypes are urine pH, specific gravity and sodium. Horizontal coordinates show coefficients from models without creatinine adjustment refitted in the same 1,757 participants; vertical coordinates show creatinine-adjusted coefficients. All models retained demographic and socioeconomic covariates and the same survey design. The dashed diagonal indicates equal coefficients, and the horizontal and vertical reference lines indicate zero. These analyses assess sensitivity to common urine concentration; full estimates are in Supplementary Table 8.
